senses.gloss: Small and weak.
examples: He was a *puny* kid who dreaded gym class.
The second batch of seedlings came up even *punier* than the first.

senses.gloss: Too small to be worth much.
examples: They offered a *puny* two percent raise.
Our marketing budget is *puny* compared to theirs.

position: both — the *nothing but* sense only before a noun: *pure luck*

senses.gloss: Not mixed with anything else.
examples: The ring is *pure* gold.
Spring water out here is *purer* than anything from a tap.

senses.gloss: Nothing but; complete — used before a noun to stress that something is only what it is.
examples: It was *pure* luck that we found the keys.
That story is *pure* nonsense.

senses.gloss: Morally clean and innocent.
examples: His motives were *pure*, whatever people said.
She had the *purest* heart of anyone in that family.

senses.gloss: Of an animal: having parents of the same breed.
examples: They paid a lot for a *purebred* German shepherd.
Is your cat *purebred* or a rescue?
*Purebred* horses come with papers.

senses.gloss: Very strict about morals, especially about pleasure and sex.
examples: Her parents were *puritanical* about dating.
The town still has a *puritanical* streak.
He's more *puritanical* about alcohol than anyone I know.

senses.gloss: Slightly purple in color.
examples: The bruise turned a *purplish* color overnight.
The sky looked more *purplish* than pink just after sunset.
She wore a *purplish* gray sweater.

senses.gloss: Built specially for one particular use.
examples: The city opened a *purpose-built* shelter downtown.
The lab is *purpose-built* for testing engines.
They practice in a *purpose-built* training facility.

contrast: *Purposeful* means *having a clear aim*. The adverb *purposely* means *on purpose*, and *purposefully* means *with determination* — *He purposely broke it* is not *He purposefully broke it*.

senses.gloss: Having a clear aim, and determined about it.
examples: She crossed the room with *purposeful* strides.
He seemed more *purposeful* after he changed jobs.
The work is hard, but it feels *purposeful*.

position: after the noun — *a notice pursuant to section 5*
contrast: Legal boilerplate, and almost always in the fixed phrase *pursuant to*. It never goes before a noun. In ordinary English say *under* or *in accordance with*.

senses.gloss: Formal and legal: in accordance with a law, rule or agreement.
examples: The records were released *pursuant to* a court order.
Payments will be made *pursuant to* the terms of the contract.
The city acted *pursuant to* its emergency powers.

senses.gloss: Trying so hard to get what you want that you annoy people.
examples: The salesman got *pushy* when we said no.
Some parents are *pushier* than others about grades.
I don't want to be *pushy*, but the deadline is Friday.

form: compound — from the phrasal verb *put upon* (to impose on someone)

senses.gloss: Feeling that other people take advantage of you or give you too much to do.
examples: She let out a long, *put-upon* sigh.
He always sounds *put-upon* when you ask for help.
The nurses feel more *put-upon* than ever after months of extra shifts.

contrast: Formal and mostly legal. In everyday English say *alleged*, *supposed* or *so-called*.

senses.gloss: Generally believed to be what the noun says, though it is not proven.
examples: The *putative* father asked for a DNA test.
Police named a *putative* motive for the attack.
The *putative* leader of the group denies any role in it.

senses.gloss: Rotting, and smelling terrible.
examples: A *putrid* smell was coming from the back of the fridge.
The water in the bottom of the cooler was *putrid*.

senses.gloss: Informal: very bad indeed.
examples: The team played a *putrid* first half.
His excuse was even more *putrid* than the last one.

contrast: Always capitalized. Note the stress: pi-thag-uh-REE-uhn, not on the first syllable.

senses.gloss: Relating to the Greek mathematician Pythagoras, especially to his theorem about right triangles.
examples: We used the *Pythagorean* theorem to find the third side.
Every geometry student memorizes the *Pythagorean* formula.
The *Pythagorean* school believed numbers ruled the universe.

contrast: Always capitalized. *A Qatari* for a person is a noun, not an adjective.

senses.gloss: From Qatar, or relating to Qatar and its people.
examples: A *Qatari* airline sponsors the tournament.
The stadium was built with *Qatari* money.
My lab partner is *Qatari*.

contrast: Also a noun (*a quack* is a fake doctor) and a verb (ducks *quack*). As an adjective it goes only before a noun: say *The remedy is a fraud*, not *The remedy is quack*.

senses.gloss: Falsely claiming to have medical knowledge or to cure people.
examples: He spent thousands on *quack* remedies.
A *quack* doctor sold them fake vitamins.
The clinic pushes *quack* cures for cancer.

senses.gloss: In math: involving a quantity multiplied by itself, that is, squared.
examples: We solved the *quadratic* equation in class.
She still remembers the *quadratic* formula from tenth grade.
The growth is *quadratic*, not linear.

contrast: Also a noun: *a square is a quadrilateral*.

senses.gloss: Having four straight sides.
examples: A trapezoid is a *quadrilateral* shape.
Draw any *quadrilateral* figure on the board.
The old fort is roughly *quadrilateral*.

contrast: Also a verb (*Sales quadrupled last year*). For the surgery and the crime the noun after it stays singular: *a quadruple bypass*, *a quadruple homicide*.

senses.gloss: Made up of four parts, or four times as big or as many.
examples: He had a *quadruple* bypass last spring.
Police are investigating a *quadruple* homicide.
She landed a *quadruple* jump in competition.

contrast: It can sound condescending: calling someone's beliefs *quaint* says they are charmingly out of date.

senses.gloss: Attractive in an old-fashioned way.
examples: They stayed in a *quaint* little inn on the coast.
It's the *quaintest* town in New England.

senses.gloss: Odd or out of date in a way that amuses you.
examples: He has a *quaint* habit of writing thank-you letters.
The idea of a landline seems *quaint* now.

contrast: A false friend. Russian *качественный* usually means *of good quality* — that is *quality* or *high-quality* in English. *Qualitative* only contrasts with *quantitative*: about kind, not about amount.

senses.gloss: Relating to the nature or kind of something rather than to amounts.
examples: The study used *qualitative* interviews instead of surveys.
There is a *qualitative* difference between the two recordings.
Her research is mostly *qualitative*.

contrast: Mostly a noun (*the quality of the work*). As an adjective it goes only before a noun; after a verb say *high-quality*: *The tools are high-quality*, not *The tools are quality*.

senses.gloss: Of a high standard.
examples: They sell *quality* furniture at a fair price.
We try to spend *quality* time together on weekends.
*Quality* childcare is hard to find here.

senses.gloss: Able to be measured or expressed in numbers.
examples: The benefits are real but not easily *quantifiable*.
Give me *quantifiable* goals for the quarter.
Air quality is more *quantifiable* than customer mood.

senses.gloss: Relating to amounts and numbers.
examples: The report includes *quantitative* data from 3,000 users.
He works on the *quantitative* side of the fund.
Their evidence is *quantitative* rather than anecdotal.

senses.gloss: Kept away from other people or animals so that a disease cannot spread.
examples: The *quarantined* passengers stayed on the ship for a week.
Our whole class was *quarantined* after the outbreak.
New birds are kept *quarantined* for thirty days.

senses.gloss: Arguing often, and looking for a fight.
examples: Two *quarrelsome* neighbors dragged the whole street into court.
He gets *quarrelsome* after a couple of drinks.
The committee is more *quarrelsome* than it used to be.

form: -ly from *quarter* — an *-ly* adjective, not an adverb here
contrast: *Quarterly* is also an adverb (*The board meets quarterly*) and a noun (a literary *quarterly*). As an adjective it stays before the noun: *the quarterly report*.

senses.gloss: Happening or produced four times a year.
examples: The *quarterly* report comes out in April.
Freelancers pay *quarterly* taxes.
She writes for a *quarterly* literary magazine.

senses.gloss: Feeling as if you might vomit.
examples: Boats make me *queasy*.
I felt *queasier* with every curve in the road.

senses.gloss: Uneasy and worried about something.
examples: Investors are *queasy* about the merger.
The whole plan gives me a *queasy* feeling.

contrast: A US bed-size word. From small to large: *twin*, *full*, *queen-size*, *king-size*. A *queen-size* bed is about 60 by 80 inches.

senses.gloss: Of a bed or bedding: fairly large — bigger than a full, smaller than a king.
examples: The room has a *queen-size* bed.
We need *queen-size* sheets, not king.
A *queen-size* mattress won't fit up those stairs.

comparison: not gradable — in the identity sense; the old *strange* sense took *queerer*, *queerest*
contrast: Once a slur, now reclaimed and used neutrally by many LGBTQ people, in academic writing and in *queer studies*. Still, do not apply it to an individual who has not used it of themselves. The *strange* sense is old-fashioned and now sounds odd in American English.

senses.gloss: Relating to people who are not heterosexual or not cisgender.
examples: She writes about *queer* history in the Midwest.
The festival celebrates *queer* artists.
He came out as *queer* in college.

senses.gloss: Old-fashioned: strange or odd.
examples: There was something *queer* about the whole story.
He felt a bit *queer* after the shot.

contrast: Not related to *query*. It describes a whiny, complaining tone, not a questioning one.

senses.gloss: Complaining in a weak, irritated way.
examples: A *querulous* voice came from the back row.
He grew *querulous* in his last years.
Her emails get more *querulous* every week.

senses.gloss: Probably not true, honest or good — worth doubting.
examples: The numbers came from a *questionable* source.
Several of the expenses look *questionable*.
His taste in movies is even more *questionable* than mine.

senses.gloss: Showing that you have doubts or want an answer.
examples: She gave me a *questioning* look.
He raised a *questioning* eyebrow.
Students today take a more *questioning* attitude toward authority.

contrast: The adverb is *quickly*. *Come quick!* is informal speech; in writing use *quickly*. *Fast* is about speed of movement, *quick* often about a short time: *a fast car*, *a quick trip*.

senses.gloss: Moving or happening fast.
examples: She's a *quick* walker — I can never keep up.
Is there a *quicker* way downtown?
He's always *quick* to blame someone else.

senses.gloss: Taking only a short time.
examples: I took a *quick* shower and left.
Can we have a *quick* word before the meeting?

senses.gloss: Able to understand and learn fast.
examples: She's *quick* — she picked up the software in a day.
He has a *quick* mind and a sharp tongue.

senses.gloss: Getting angry very easily.
examples: His father was *quick-tempered* and everyone in town knew it.
She's less *quick-tempered* than she was at twenty.
A *quick-tempered* coach can lose a locker room fast.

senses.gloss: Able to think and answer fast, often in a funny way.
examples: The host is *quick-witted* and never loses the room.
A *quick-witted* clerk stopped the scam.
You have to be more *quick-witted* than that to do stand-up.

senses.gloss: Made of two layers of cloth sewn together with padding in between.
examples: She wore a *quilted* jacket over her sweater.
The bedspread is *quilted* by hand.
*Quilted* oven mitts protect your hands better.

comparison: not gradable — it already means *the most typical*
form: from *quintessence* — the purest form of something

senses.gloss: Being the most perfect example of a type.
examples: He's the *quintessential* New Yorker — loud, kind, always late.
Diners are the *quintessential* American restaurant.
That album is *quintessential* seventies rock.

senses.gloss: Unusual in a likable, slightly odd way.
examples: It's a *quirky* little bookstore with a cat in the window.
Her second novel is even *quirkier* than the first.
He has a *quirky* sense of humor.

contrast: The pronunciation does not follow the name: kwik-SAH-tik, not kee-HOH-tik.

senses.gloss: Having generous, idealistic plans that have almost no chance of working.
examples: He launched a *quixotic* run for governor.
The plan is noble but more *quixotic* than practical.
Her *quixotic* campaign to save the old theater lasted two years.

senses.gloss: Showing that you are puzzled, often with some amusement.
examples: He gave her a *quizzical* look.
She raised one eyebrow in a *quizzical* expression.
The second question got an even more *quizzical* look than the first.

senses.gloss: Worth quoting, or saying things that people like to repeat.
examples: The coach is endlessly *quotable*.
It's the most *quotable* movie of the decade.
He wrote a short, *quotable* line for the poster.

form: compound — noun + *-ing* participle; a *rabble* is a disorderly crowd

senses.gloss: Stirring up the anger of a crowd, usually for political ends.
examples: He gave a *rabble-rousing* speech outside the capitol.
The paper called her a *rabble-rousing* populist.
His second speech was even more *rabble-rousing* than the first.

position: both — the *rabies* sense mostly before a noun

senses.gloss: Extreme and fanatical in your opinions or support.
examples: He's a *rabid* Yankees fan.
The bill faces *rabid* opposition in the Senate.
Her most *rabid* supporters lined up at five in the morning.

senses.gloss: Of an animal: having rabies.
examples: A *rabid* raccoon bit the neighbor's dog.
Animal control caught a *rabid* fox behind the school.

contrast: *Racial* is neutral and simply names the category (*racial demographics*). *Racist* is a judgment: it means based on prejudice. *A racial comment* is not the same as *a racist comment*.

senses.gloss: Relating to race, or to relations between races.
examples: The city studied *racial* disparities in housing.
*Racial* profiling is against department policy.
They talked about *racial* justice in the classroom.

contrast: Also a noun (*He's a racist*). Keep it apart from the neutral *racial*.

senses.gloss: Showing or based on prejudice against people of another race.
examples: He was fired for a *racist* joke.
The policy had a *racist* effect, whatever its intent.
His later columns were even more openly *racist*.

contrast: Nothing to do with *race* the contest or *race* the group of people — it means mildly sexual.

senses.gloss: Slightly shocking, usually because of sexual content.
examples: The novel was considered *racy* in 1955.
She posted a *racier* photo than usual.
It's a *racy* comedy — don't watch it with your parents.

senses.gloss: Looking very happy, in a way that shows on your face.
examples: The bride looked *radiant*.
She gave us the most *radiant* smile.
He was *radiant* with pride at the ceremony.

senses.gloss: Sending out light or heat.
examples: *Radiant* heat from the floor warms the whole room.
The *radiant* glow of the fire filled the cabin.

contrast: Also a noun (*a radical*). Beyond the political meaning that Russian *радикальный* shares, English *radical* often just means *thorough and far-reaching*: *a radical redesign* is not a political statement.

senses.gloss: Complete and far-reaching, especially of a change.
examples: The company made *radical* changes to the schedule.
We need a more *radical* rethink of the budget.
She had *radical* surgery and recovered well.

senses.gloss: Supporting extreme political or social change.
examples: She joined a *radical* student group in the seventies.
His views got more *radical* over the years.

form: compound — noun + participle; often shortened to *RC*

senses.gloss: Operated from a distance by radio signals.
examples: He flies a *radio-controlled* plane on weekends.
The gate at the end of the driveway is *radio-controlled*.
*Radio-controlled* cars were the big gift that Christmas.

senses.gloss: Giving off harmful radiation.
examples: The site is still *radioactive* forty years later.
They store the *radioactive* waste underground.
Some of the soil is more *radioactive* than the air above it.

senses.gloss: So controversial that politicians avoid touching it.
examples: Social Security is *radioactive* in an election year.
The topic became *radioactive* after the scandal.

contrast: Two syllables: RAG-id, like *rugged* and *wicked*. In *run ragged* it means worn out from overwork: *The twins run me ragged*.

senses.gloss: Torn, old and in bad condition.
examples: He wore a *ragged* T-shirt and no shoes.
The flag was *ragged* at the edges after the storm.

senses.gloss: Uneven and rough, not smooth or controlled.
examples: The team's play was *ragged* in the first quarter.
She took a *ragged* breath and kept going.
His singing got more *ragged* toward the end of the tour.

senses.gloss: Very strong and violent, of fire, water or weather.
examples: A *raging* fire destroyed the barn.
They had to cross a *raging* river.

senses.gloss: Very intense, of pain, thirst or an argument.
examples: I woke up with a *raging* headache.
There's a *raging* debate about the new rules.

contrast: *Save it for a rainy day* means save money for a time when you will need it.

senses.gloss: With a lot of rain.
examples: It was a cold, *rainy* Tuesday in March.
October was *rainier* than usual this year.
The whole week is supposed to be *rainy*.

contrast: *Raised voices* means loud and angry ones. *She was raised in Ohio* is the verb, not this adjective.

senses.gloss: Higher than the surface around it.
examples: We built a *raised* garden bed out of cedar.
The band played on a *raised* platform at the end of the room.
*Raised* lettering runs across the cover.

senses.gloss: Long and confused, with no clear point.
examples: He left a *rambling* voicemail at two in the morning.
The essay is *rambling* and hard to follow.
Her second speech was even more *rambling* than the first.

senses.gloss: Of a house or garden: spread out in an irregular way.
examples: They bought a *rambling* old farmhouse with six bedrooms.
A *rambling* rose covers the back fence.

contrast: American English. British speakers say *rumbustious*.

senses.gloss: Noisy, full of energy and hard to control, usually of children or animals.
examples: Three *rambunctious* boys tore through the kitchen.
The puppy gets *rambunctious* right before dinner.
The crowd was more *rambunctious* than security expected.

contrast: Almost always about something bad that is spreading: *rampant inflation*, *rampant corruption*, never *rampant kindness*.

senses.gloss: Spreading fast and out of control.
examples: Corruption was more *rampant* in that department than anywhere else in the city.
*Rampant* inflation wiped out their savings.
Rumors ran *rampant* after the announcement.

senses.gloss: Badly built or falling apart; of an organization, thrown together and barely working.
examples: They spent the summer in a *ramshackle* cabin by the river.
The porch looked even more *ramshackle* up close.
It's a *ramshackle* operation — nobody knows who's in charge.

contrast: *Rancid* is for fats and oils. Milk goes *sour*, meat goes *bad* or is *spoiled*, bread goes *stale*.

senses.gloss: Of fat, oil or butter: old, and tasting or smelling unpleasant.
examples: The peanut butter went *rancid* in the heat.
There's a *rancid* smell coming from that pan.
Nuts turn *rancid* faster than most people think.

senses.gloss: Full of bitter, long-lasting anger.
examples: The divorce was long and *rancorous*.
A *rancorous* debate split the board in half.
Talks grew more *rancorous* with every week that passed.

contrast: *At random* is a fixed phrase: *We picked names at random*. The informal *strange* sense is common in speech but out of place in formal writing.

senses.gloss: Chosen or happening with no plan or pattern.
examples: They called ten *random* names from the list.
The attacks look *random*, but the police aren't sure.
Each student gets a *random* seat assignment.

senses.gloss: Informal: strange, unexpected or out of place.
senses.ru: странный, ни с того ни с сего
examples: Some *random* guy started talking to me on the bus.
That was the most *random* thing he's ever said.

contrast: American spelling *-ized*; British writing often has *randomised*.

senses.gloss: Arranged or assigned by chance, especially in research.
examples: It was a *randomized* controlled trial with 400 patients.
Each group got a *randomized* list of tasks.
Students took a *randomized* version of the test.

position: both — the *complete* sense only before a noun: *a rank amateur*
contrast: Also a noun (*military rank*) and a verb (*The team ranks third*).

senses.gloss: Complete and total — used before a noun to stress how bad something is.
examples: He's a *rank* amateur with a camera.
That's *rank* hypocrisy and everyone knows it.
It was *rank* stupidity to drive in that storm.

senses.gloss: Smelling strong and unpleasant.
examples: His gym bag smelled even more *rank* after a week in the car.
*Rank* water sat in the bottom of the cooler.

position: both — usually in compounds before a noun: *top-ranked*

senses.gloss: Given a position on an official list of the best.
examples: She's the third-*ranked* player in the world.
Only *ranked* teams make the tournament.
He lost to a lower-*ranked* opponent in the second round.

contrast: Also a noun (*the world rankings*). Don't confuse it with *ranked*: the *ranking* officer is the most senior one, a *ranked* player has a number next to their name.

senses.gloss: Holding the highest position in a group; most senior.
examples: The *ranking* officer took over the scene.
She's the *ranking* Democrat on the committee.
Several high-*ranking* officials resigned that week.

senses.gloss: Greedy, taking as much as possible with no concern for anyone else.
examples: *Rapacious* lenders went after older homeowners.
He wrote about the *rapacious* side of the timber industry.
The company grew more *rapacious* as it lost market share.

contrast: *Rapid* describes changes and processes. For people, cars and answers, American English says *fast* or *quick*: *a fast runner*, not *a rapid runner*.

senses.gloss: Happening fast, especially of change or growth.
examples: The town saw *rapid* growth after the plant opened.
She made a *rapid* recovery from surgery.
Change has been more *rapid* than anyone predicted.

contrast: Sounds exactly like *wrapped* but is a different word. The set phrase is *rapt attention*.

senses.gloss: So interested in something that you notice nothing else.
examples: The kids listened with *rapt* attention.
She sat *rapt* through the whole concert.
A *rapt* audience filled every seat in the hall.

senses.gloss: Showing great delight and enthusiasm.
examples: The band got a *rapturous* welcome in Chicago.
Critics were even more *rapturous* about her second novel.
*Rapturous* applause went on for five minutes.

takes: *for* + noun + *to*-infinitive — *It's rare for him to call*
contrast: Russian *редкий* also covers hair and combs; English uses *thin* for hair (*thinning hair*) and *fine-toothed* for combs. For meat the scale is *rare*, *medium rare*, *medium*, *medium well*, *well done*.

senses.gloss: Not often seen, found or done.
examples: Snow is *rarer* here than it used to be.
It's *rare* for him to call on a weekday.
The museum owns a *rare* first edition.

senses.gloss: Of beef: cooked only a little, still red inside.
examples: He orders his steak *rare*.
I asked for medium, not *rare*.

form: -ed from *rarefy* — to make thinner; note the spelling *rarefied*, not *rarified*

senses.gloss: Belonging to a small, closed world that few people enter.
examples: He moved in the *rarefied* world of art collecting.
Rare book dealing is an even more *rarefied* world than art collecting.

senses.gloss: Of air: thin, with less oxygen than usual.
examples: Climbers struggle in the *rarefied* air above 15,000 feet.
The *rarefied* atmosphere makes every step harder.

contrast: Nearly always in the fixed phrase *raring to go*. It never goes before a noun, and it is not related to *rare*.

senses.gloss: Very eager to start something.
examples: The team was *raring* to go by kickoff.
She's *raring* to get back on the court.
We were up at six and *raring* to start.

takes: *of* + person + *to*-infinitive — *It was rash of him to quit*
contrast: Also a noun: *a skin rash*, and *a rash of* means a sudden series of something bad (*a rash of break-ins*).

senses.gloss: Done or acting too quickly, without thinking about what will happen.
examples: Don't make any *rash* decisions while you're angry.
It was *rash* of him to quit without another job lined up.
It would be even more *rash* to sell the house now.

form: -y from *rasp* — a rough file, and the sound one makes

senses.gloss: Rough and harsh in sound, of a voice or of breathing.
examples: He has a *raspy* voice from years of smoking.
Her breathing got *raspier* through the night.
The singer's *raspy* tone is her signature.

form: from *Ras Tafari*, the name of Haile Selassie before he became emperor
contrast: Always capitalized. Also a noun (*a Rastafarian*), often shortened to *Rasta*.

senses.gloss: Relating to Rastafari, a religious movement that began in Jamaica in the 1930s.
examples: *Rastafarian* beliefs shaped early reggae.
She studies *Rastafarian* communities in Jamaica.
The red, gold and green stripes are *Rastafarian* colors.

contrast: Don't mix it up with the noun *rationale* (ruh-shuh-NAL), which means the reasoning behind a decision.

senses.gloss: Based on clear thinking rather than on emotion; able to think clearly.
examples: There's a perfectly *rational* explanation for the noise.
Try to be *rational* about the money.
Her argument is more *rational* than his, even if it's less popular.

form: -ed from *rattle* — what shakes you shakes your nerves

senses.gloss: Nervous and upset after something unsettling.
examples: She sounded *rattled* on the phone.
The pitcher got *rattled* after the error.
He was more *rattled* by the question than he let on.

contrast: In American English it means *worn out*. In British English *ratty* can mean *irritable*.

senses.gloss: Old, worn out and in bad condition.
examples: He still wears that *ratty* old hoodie.
The couch is even *rattier* than I remembered.
*Ratty* carpet covered the stairs.

senses.gloss: Loud and rough, especially of a crowd, laughter or a party.
examples: A *raucous* crowd filled the bar after the game.
There was *raucous* laughter from the back of the room.
The party got more *raucous* as the night went on.

senses.gloss: Rude and sexual in a crude way.
examples: The comedian's set was pretty *raunchy*.
Her jokes get *raunchier* after midnight.
It's a *raunchy* movie, not one for the family.

senses.gloss: Badly damaged or almost destroyed.
examples: They flew supplies into the *ravaged* coastal towns.
His face was *ravaged* by years of hard living.
The *ravaged* forest will take decades to grow back.

contrast: Nothing to do with the bird *raven*. It is much stronger than *hungry* — closer to *starving*.

senses.gloss: Extremely hungry.
examples: The kids were *ravenous* after practice.
By dinnertime they were even more *ravenous*.
He ate like a *ravenous* teenager.

form: fixed phrase — *raving* used as an intensifier + *mad*; the full form is *stark raving mad*
contrast: A fixed phrase, and it goes after a verb, not before a noun. Here *mad* means *crazy*, not *angry* — though people also use the whole phrase for great anger.

senses.gloss: Completely crazy, or wild with anger.
examples: By the third day of delays he was *raving mad*.
You'd have to be *raving mad* to swim in that water.
She went stark *raving mad* trying to fix the printer.

contrast: Literary and a little old-fashioned, and usually about beauty. The verb *ravish* has a dark second meaning, but the adjective does not carry it.

senses.gloss: Extremely beautiful.
examples: She looked *ravishing* in the green dress.
The garden is *ravishing* in June.
He painted the most *ravishing* sunset I've ever seen.

contrast: *A raw deal* means unfair treatment. *Raw* meat is uncooked; meat that has gone bad is *spoiled*.

senses.gloss: Not cooked.
examples: Don't eat *raw* cookie dough.
The fish is served *raw*, with rice and ginger.

senses.gloss: Not yet processed, cleaned up or analyzed.
examples: The lab sent us the *raw* data.
*Raw* materials cost more this year than last.

senses.gloss: Of skin: sore, red and painful.
examples: His hands were *raw* from the rope.
My throat felt *raw* after shouting all night.

senses.gloss: Honest and full of strong feeling, with nothing softened.
examples: It's the *rawest* song on the album.
The interview was *raw* and uncomfortable to watch.

senses.gloss: Extremely sharp.
examples: The knife is *razor-sharp*, so be careful.
*Razor-sharp* rocks line that stretch of the shore.

senses.gloss: Very quick and precise, of a mind, memory or sense of humor.
examples: At ninety she's still *razor-sharp*.
He has a *razor-sharp* memory for names.

senses.gloss: Able to be contacted.
examples: I'm *reachable* by text all weekend.
She's more *reachable* by text than by phone.

senses.gloss: Able to be got to or achieved.
examples: The summit is *reachable* in a single day.
The goal is ambitious but *reachable*.

contrast: Always a criticism, never a neutral label. It is not the same as *reactive*: a *reactionary* politician wants the past back, a *reactive* one only responds to events.

senses.gloss: Opposing social or political change, and wanting things to go back to how they were.
examples: The editorial called the ruling *reactionary*.
He joined a *reactionary* faction of the party.
Her politics grew more *reactionary* with age.

senses.gloss: Responding to events after they happen instead of planning ahead.
examples: Management is *reactive* — nothing gets fixed until it breaks.
We need to be less *reactive* and more strategic.
It was a *reactive* decision made in one afternoon.

senses.gloss: In chemistry: easily taking part in chemical reactions.
examples: Sodium is highly *reactive* with water.
Store the *reactive* chemicals in a separate cabinet.

contrast: *Readable* praises the writing; *legible* is only about whether the letters can be made out.

senses.gloss: Enjoyable and easy to read.
examples: It's a dense subject, but the book is very *readable*.
She writes the most *readable* science column around.

senses.gloss: Clear enough to be read.
examples: The sign is barely *readable* from the road.
Make the font bigger so it's *readable* on a phone.

senses.gloss: Already made and ready to use, rather than made to order.
examples: We bought a *ready-made* pie crust.
He had a *ready-made* excuse waiting.
*Ready-made* curtains rarely fit these windows.

senses.gloss: Already cooked or prepared, so you can eat it right away.
examples: The store sells *ready-to-eat* meals by the register.
Pack some *ready-to-eat* snacks for the drive.
The salad is washed and *ready-to-eat*.

senses.gloss: Of clothing: made in standard sizes rather than for one person.
examples: The designer launched a *ready-to-wear* line last fall.
*Ready-to-wear* suits usually need some tailoring anyway.
Everything in this part of the store is *ready-to-wear*.

position: both — the emphasizing sense only before a noun: *a real problem*
contrast: *Real good* and *real fast* are informal speech; in writing use the adverb *really*. *For real* is also informal.

senses.gloss: Actually existing, not imagined or invented.
examples: Is the threat *real*, or is it just talk?
The dream felt more *real* than the morning did.

senses.gloss: Genuine, not a copy or an imitation.
examples: The bag is *real* leather.
Those aren't *real* diamonds.

senses.gloss: Used before a noun to stress how much something is what it is.
examples: The parking downtown is a *real* problem.
He can be a *real* pain when he's tired.

contrast: Hyphenated before a noun, two separate words after a verb: *real-time updates*, but *The data arrives in real time*.

senses.gloss: Happening or shown at the same moment as the event itself.
examples: The app gives *real-time* traffic updates.
We get *real-time* data from the sensors on the bridge.
*Real-time* translation is built into the phone.

senses.gloss: Sensible about what is actually possible.
examples: Let's set a *realistic* deadline.
Be *realistic* about how much you can finish by Friday.
Her expectations are more *realistic* now than they were.

senses.gloss: Looking or sounding like real life.
examples: The special effects are surprisingly *realistic*.
He paints in a *realistic* style.

contrast: *Realize* is usually a verb (*I realized my mistake*). As an adjective it turns up in *fully realized* and in finance, where *realized* gains are ones you have actually taken.

senses.gloss: Made real and worked out in full.
examples: It's a fully *realized* vision of the city in 2100.
The characters feel like *realized* people, not sketches.

senses.gloss: In finance: actually received or lost, not just on paper.
examples: You pay tax on *realized* gains, not on paper ones.
*Realized* losses can offset those gains.

contrast: Also a noun (*the rear of the building*) and a verb (*to rear children*). As an adjective it never follows a verb: say *The door at the back is locked*, not *The door is rear*.

senses.gloss: At or in the back of something.
examples: The *rear* door doesn't lock properly.
Passengers exit through the *rear* entrance.
Check the *rear* tires for wear.

senses.gloss: Fair and sensible.
examples: That sounds like a *reasonable* request.
Be *reasonable* — he's only nine.
A more *reasonable* boss would have let it go.

senses.gloss: Fairly good or fairly large, though not outstanding.
examples: We had a *reasonable* turnout for a rainy night.
She has a *reasonable* chance of winning the seat.

senses.gloss: Not too expensive.
examples: The hotel was clean and *reasonable*.
They charge *reasonable* prices for repairs.

contrast: *Reasoned* is about the argument — carefully built. *Reasonable* is about the person or the demand — fair and sensible.

senses.gloss: Based on careful thinking and clear argument.
examples: She wrote a *reasoned* response to the criticism.
The judge gave a carefully *reasoned* opinion.
We need a more *reasoned* debate about the bill.
